pos: n. (a fleet of ships; in Scripture always Solomon's, built with Tyrian help and sailing for gold)
etymology: Old French navie, from Latin navis, a ship. Israel was never a seafaring people; the word enters the Bible with Solomon, and it enters with a foreign partner.
biblical_def: “And king Solomon made a navy of ships in Eziongeber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red sea, in the land of Edom” (1Ki 9:26), and he could not sail it alone: “Hiram sent in the navy his servants, shipmen that had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon” (1Ki 9:27). The cargo was gold — “they came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents” (1Ki 9:28) — and afterwards “great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones” (1Ki 10:11). At its height: “the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram” (1Ki 10:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a navy as a fleet of ships; an assemblage of merchantmen; or the whole of the ships of war belonging to a nation or king.
webster_full: NAVY, n. A fleet of ships; an assemblage of merchantmen, or so many as sail in company.
NAVY, n. The whole of the ships of war belonging to a nation or king.
FLEET, n. A navy or squadron of ships; a number of ships in company.
scriptures: And king Solomon made a navy of ships in Eziongeber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red sea, in the land of Edom.
And Hiram sent in the navy his servants, shipmen that had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon.
And they came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and brought it to king Solomon.
For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks.
corruption_summary: Solomon's fleet is described admiringly and belongs to a chapter-long inventory that Deuteronomy 17 had forbidden in advance.
corruption_paragraphs: First Kings 9 and 10 are written to impress and to indict at the same time. The navy at Eziongeber, the Tyrian sailors, the gold of Ophir, the three-year voyages, the silver made as stones in Jerusalem — every item is reported with evident wonder, and the whole catalogue reads as a checklist against the king's law in Deuteronomy 17, which forbade multiplying horses, wives, and silver and gold. Chapter 11 delivers the verdict without softening it: his wives turned away his heart after other gods. The Holy Spirit lets the splendour stand at full height before pulling it down, which is a more devastating structure than any warning could have been.

The corruption to name is the reading of prosperity as endorsement, and the sharpest form of it in the church is the doctrine that God's favour shows itself in increase. Solomon had more than any man before or after and finished his reign building high places for Chemosh on the hill before Jerusalem. Ecclesiastes is his own testimony on the matter, and its verdict on everything the navy brought home is vanity and vexation of spirit. The wisdom to draw is not that wealth is evil — Scripture never says so — but that it is a dangerous trust, and that a heart is more easily lost in plenty than in want.
roots_summary: Hebrew oni (H590), fleet, navy of ships; sapan / anshey oniyyot, shipmen; Ophir (H211), the gold-bearing port.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ophir (H211) — Ophir, source of fine gold; 1 Kings 9:28, Job 22:24, Psalm 45:9.
usage: “King Solomon made a navy of ships in Eziongeber” — Israel's one venture at sea.
“Shipmen that had knowledge of the sea” — supplied by Hiram, not by Israel.
“A navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram” — the height of the reign.

pos: n. (a small craft; in Acts 27 the ship's tender by which the sailors tried to desert)
etymology: Old English bat. In the KJV the word is not the fishing vessel of the Gospels (which is a ship) but a small boat — a ferry across Jordan, and the skiff towed behind a grain freighter in the Adria.
biblical_def: A ferry brings David home: “there went over a ferry boat to carry over the king's household… And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king” (2Sa 19:18). The rest of the word's life is in one storm. Off Clauda, “we had much work to come by the boat” (Act 27:16). Later the sailors tried to escape in it: “when they had let down the boat into the sea, under colour as though they would have cast anchors out of the foreship” (Act 27:30). Paul saw it: “Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” (Act 27:31). “Then the soldiers cut off the ropes of the boat, and let her fall off” (Act 27:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a boat as a small open vessel or watercraft, usually moved by oars or rowing, and also the small boat carried by a ship.
webster_full: BOAT, n. A small open vessel, or water craft, usually moved by oars or rowing.
BOAT, n. A small vessel carried by a ship, for the use of the crew; as the long boat, the yawl.
FERRY-BOAT, n. A boat for conveying passengers over a river or other water.
scriptures: And there went over a ferry boat to carry over the king's household, and to do what he thought good. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was come over Jordan;
And as the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship, when they had let down the boat into the sea, under colour as though they would have cast anchors out of the foreship,
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
Then the soldiers cut off the ropes of the boat, and let her fall off.
corruption_summary: God had promised Paul every life aboard, and Paul still insisted the sailors stay, which is how Scripture holds decree and means together.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 27 is the clearest narrative case in the New Testament for the compatibility of an absolute promise with necessary means. An angel had told Paul plainly: God hath given thee all them that sail with thee; and Paul had announced it to the ship — there shall be no loss of any man's life among you. Then the sailors tried to slip away in the boat, and Paul said, except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved. The promise was certain and the seamanship was necessary, and the apostle saw no conflict. The soldiers cut the ropes, the crew stayed, and every soul reached land.

The corruption to name is fatalism dressed as faith — the reasoning that if God has decreed the end, the means are optional. It is not the doctrine of providence but its caricature, and Acts 27 refutes it in a working example. The Reformed confessions have always said that God ordains the means along with the end, which is why prayer, preaching, medicine, and ordinary competence are commanded rather than dispensed with. The opposite error is in the same chapter: the centurion at first believed the master and owner of the ship more than the things which were spoken by Paul, and it cost them the cargo.
roots_summary: Greek skaphe (G4627), a small boat, ship's tender; ploion (G4143), ship; Hebrew abarah (H5679), a ferry, crossing place.
roots_lines: Hebrew abarah (H5679) — ferry boat, crossing; 2 Samuel 19:18 only.
Greek prophasis (G4392) — pretence, colour, pretext; Acts 27:30, Mark 12:40.
Greek sozo (G4982) — to save, preserve; Acts 27:31, Romans 10:9.
usage: “Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” — a promise and its means.
“The soldiers cut off the ropes of the boat, and let her fall off.”
“There went over a ferry boat to carry over the king's household” — David's return.

pos: n. pl. (steersmen; those who guided the ships of Tyre, and who mourn her fall)
etymology: Old French pilot, ultimately from Greek pedon, a rudder or oar-blade. The Hebrew of Ezekiel is chobel, from a root for a rope or cable — the man who handles the ship's tackling.
biblical_def: Ezekiel's lamentation for Tyre is built as a ship. “The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots” (Eze 27:8). The wreck takes everyone: “thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise… shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin” (Eze 27:27). Then the survivors on shore: “The suburbs shall shake at the sound of the cry of thy pilots” (Eze 27:28), and “all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land” (Eze 27:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pilot as one who steers a ship, and particularly one whose office is to steer a ship into or out of port, or in dangerous navigation.
webster_full: PILOT, n. One whose office or occupation is to steer ships, particularly along a coast, or into and out of a harbor.
PILOT, v.t. To direct the course of a ship in a dangerous navigation.
MARINER, n. A seaman or sailor; one whose occupation is to assist in navigating ships.
scriptures: Eze 27:8
The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots.
Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas.

Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin.
And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land;
corruption_summary: Tyre's own rowers brought her into great waters, and the ruin came from the direction her strength was pointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 27:26 is the hinge of the lamentation and one of the most quotable lines in the prophets: Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas. Tyre was not ruined by weakness. Her rowers were excellent, her pilots were her wise men, and they took her further out than anyone had gone — and that is where the east wind found her. The next chapter names the sin under the seamanship: thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches; thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas.

The corruption to name is competence without the fear of God, which Scripture treats not as neutral but as the accelerant of ruin. Tyre's judgment is not for incompetence and not for poverty; it is for a pride that grew directly out of genuine skill and real success. Ezekiel 28 traces the pattern behind it in language the church has long read as reaching past the prince of Tyre to the fall that stands behind every such fall. The doctrine for ordinary use is Proverbs' — pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall — and the picture for it is a first-rate crew rowing hard into open sea.
roots_summary: Hebrew chobel (H2259), pilot, sailor who handles the ropes; mallach (H4419), mariner; qadim (H6921), the east wind.
roots_lines: Hebrew gaboah (H1364) — high, lifted up, proud; Ezekiel 28:2, Proverbs 16:18.
usage: “Thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots.”
“Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters” — ruin by way of strength.
“The suburbs shall shake at the sound of the cry of thy pilots.”

pos: n. pl. (the Persian satraps; the king's deputies over the provinces)
etymology: Old French lieu tenant, place-holder — one who holds a place in another's stead. The KJV uses it for the Persian achashdarpan, the satrap of an imperial province.
biblical_def: Ezra carries the king's authority into hostile country: “they delivered the king's commissions unto the king's lieutenants, and to the governors on this side the river: and they furthered the people, and the house of God” (Ezr 8:36). Esther records the same officials on the day the tables turned: “all the rulers of the provinces, and the lieutenants, and the deputies, and officers of the king, helped the Jews; because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them” (Est 9:3) — the man they now feared having been, a short time before, paraded through the street by the enemy who built his gallows (Est 6:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lieutenant as an officer who supplies the place of a superior in his absence; one who acts by vicarious authority.
webster_full: LIEUTENANT, n. An officer who supplies the place of a superior in his absence; a deputy.
LIEUTENANT, n. In military affairs, the second commissioned officer in a company of infantry, cavalry or artillery.
DEPUTY, n. A person appointed or elected to act for another; a substitute in office.
scriptures: Ezr 8:36
And they delivered the king's commissions unto the king's lieutenants, and to the governors on this side the river: and they furthered the people, and the house of God.
Est 6:11

Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.
Est 8:15

And Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal apparel of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold, and with a garment of fine linen and purple: and the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad.
Est 9:3
And all the rulers of the provinces, and the lieutenants, and the deputies, and officers of the king, helped the Jews; because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them.
corruption_summary: Persian officials furthered the house of God and helped the Jews, which is how Scripture describes God governing His people through a bureaucracy that never knew Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra and Esther are the books of the hidden hand. There is no pillar of fire in either, no prophet doing signs, no army of the LORD. There are commissions, satraps, letters sealed with the king's ring, a sleepless night, and a book of records read aloud. And through that machinery the house of God is built and a nation is preserved. Ezra says it plainly — the hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him — and then describes the good arriving in the form of a Persian filing system. Esther never mentions God's name and is about nothing else.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that providence is usually administrative. Believers are trained by the dramatic passages of Scripture to look for deliverance shaped like the Red Sea, and most deliverance in Scripture, and nearly all of it in ordinary life, looks like Ezra 8:36 — officials who furthered the people, for reasons of their own, at the right moment. The prayer of Ezra 8:21, fasting at the river Ahava for a right way, was answered by a safe road and cooperative civil servants. That is not a lesser answer.
roots_summary: Hebrew achashdarpan (H323), satrap, lieutenant of a Persian province; pechah (H6346), governor; dath (H1881), decree, commission.
roots_lines: Hebrew dath (H1881) — decree, law, commission; Ezra 8:36, Esther 1:19.
Hebrew nasa (H5375) — to lift up, further, support; Ezra 8:36, 1:4.
usage: “They furthered the people, and the house of God” — Persian officials, God's purpose.
“The lieutenants, and the deputies, and officers of the king, helped the Jews.”
“Because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them” — the reason given.

pos: n. pl. (siege works thrown up against a city; the towers and mounds of a besieging army)
etymology: Latin fortis, strong, through Old French fort. In the KJV the forts are usually the besieger's works rather than the defender's — the mounds and towers raised to break a wall down.
biblical_def: The word marks the beginning of the end for Jerusalem: “Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he, and all his host, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it; and they built forts against it round about” (2Ki 25:1), “And the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah” (2Ki 25:2), and Jeremiah records the same day and the same works (Jer 52:4). Isaiah had announced it a century earlier in God's own voice: “I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee” (Isa 29:3). And Isaiah saw beyond it: “the forts and towers shall be for dens for ever, a joy of wild asses, a pasture of flocks” (Isa 32:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fort as a fortified place; a place surrounded with a ditch, rampart and parapet, to be defended against an enemy; a fortress.
webster_full: FORT, n. A fortified place; a place surrounded with a ditch, rampart and parapet, or with palisades, stockades or other means of defense.
FORTIFY, v.t. To surround with a wall, ditch, or other works, with a view to defend against the attacks of an enemy.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
scriptures: And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he, and all his host, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it; and they built forts against it round about.
And the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah.
Isa 29:3
And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee.
Because the palaces shall be forsaken; the multitude of the city shall be left; the forts and towers shall be for dens for ever, a joy of wild asses, a pasture of flocks;
corruption_summary: Isaiah 29:3 puts the siege works in God's own hands — I will raise forts against thee — before Babylon ever marched.
corruption_paragraphs: The grammar of Isaiah 29:3 is what makes it terrible. Not the Babylonians will raise forts but I will raise forts against thee. God claims the siege of His own city as His own act. The chapter has already said why: this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men. Formalism is answered by a siege. And the same God who raises the works promises in the same chapter that the multitude of the enemy shall be as small dust, so that the judgment and the deliverance are alike His.

The corruption to name is worship reduced to precept — the very thing Isaiah 29:13 diagnoses, and the verse Christ quoted against the Pharisees in Matthew 15. A church can retain every external of orthodox worship while the heart has been removed far off, and the outward correctness makes the condition harder to detect, not easier. The Reformed emphasis on the affections in worship is not a concession to sentiment but obedience to this text: God requires the heart, and a fear of Him learned by human rule rather than by His word is what He raised forts against.
roots_summary: Hebrew dayeq (H1785), siege wall, fort; solelah (H5550), mount, siege ramp; matsor (H4692), siege, entrenchment.
roots_lines: Hebrew dayeq (H1785) — siege fort, bulwark; 2 Kings 25:1, Jeremiah 52:4, Ezekiel 17:17.
Hebrew solelah (H5550) — mount, siege ramp; Isaiah 29:3, 2 Samuel 20:15.
usage: “They built forts against it round about” — the last siege of Jerusalem.
“I will raise forts against thee” — the LORD claiming the siege as His own.
“The forts and towers shall be for dens for ever” — what the works become.

pos: n. (a body of men lying in wait; a concealed force set behind an enemy)
etymology: Old French embuscher, to set in the wood, from busche, a log. The KJV form with -ment names the company itself rather than the act — the men in hiding.
biblical_def: “But Jeroboam caused an ambushment to come about behind them: so they were before Judah, and the ambushment was behind them” (2Ch 13:13). The trap worked and the battle was still lost: “when Judah looked back, behold, the battle was before and behind: and they cried unto the LORD, and the priests sounded with the trumpets” (2Ch 13:14); “Then the men of Judah gave a shout: and as the men of Judah shouted, it came to pass, that God smote Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah” (2Ch 13:15). The chronicler states the cause: “the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers” (2Ch 13:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ambush as a private or concealed station where troops lie in wait to attack by surprise, and the troops so posted.
webster_full: AMBUSH, n. A private or concealed station, where troops lie in wait to attack their enemy by surprise.
AMBUSH, n. The troops posted in a concealed place, for attacking by surprise; a lying in wait.
AMBUSHMENT, n. An ambush; the state of lying in wait for the purpose of attacking by surprise.
scriptures: But Jeroboam caused an ambushment to come about behind them: so they were before Judah, and the ambushment was behind them.
And when Judah looked back, behold, the battle was before and behind: and they cried unto the LORD, and the priests sounded with the trumpets.
Then the men of Judah gave a shout: and as the men of Judah shouted, it came to pass, that God smote Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.
Thus the children of Israel were brought under at that time, and the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers.
corruption_summary: Judah was outnumbered two to one and surrounded, and the chronicler gives the whole reason for the victory in one clause: they relied upon the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Chronicles 13 is careful with its numbers — four hundred thousand against eight hundred thousand — and careful with its causes. Jeroboam's tactics were superior; the ambushment closed behind Judah exactly as planned; the battle was before and behind. And Judah cried unto the LORD, the priests sounded the trumpets, the men shouted, and God smote Jeroboam. The chronicler will not let the reader attribute the outcome to anything else: they prevailed because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers. Chronicles is written for a post-exilic people who needed exactly this lesson about where strength comes from.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reliance is a definite act rather than a mood. Judah did not merely feel dependent; they cried out, they sounded the trumpets God had appointed, and they went forward. Abijah's speech before the battle is a plain doctrinal argument about the covenant, the priesthood, and the golden calves Jeroboam had made, and the reliance follows from what he says is true. Faith in Scripture is always faith in something asserted. The men surrounded on the field were relying on a God they had just heard described.
roots_summary: Hebrew maarab (H3993), ambush, lying in wait; zaaq (H2199), to cry out; shaan (H8172), to lean upon, rely.
roots_lines: Hebrew maarab (H3993) — ambush, lying in wait; 2 Chronicles 13:13, Joshua 8:9.
Hebrew zaaq (H2199) — to cry out, call for help; 2 Chronicles 13:14, Exodus 2:23.
Hebrew shaan (H8172) — to lean, rely upon; 2 Chronicles 13:18, Proverbs 3:5.
Hebrew nagaph (H5062) — to smite, strike; 2 Chronicles 13:15, 2 Chronicles 14:12.
usage: “The ambushment was behind them” — Judah surrounded by design.
“They cried unto the LORD, and the priests sounded with the trumpets.”
“Because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers” — the stated cause.

pos: n. pl. (peoples put under forced tribute or labour instead of being driven out)
etymology: Latin tributarius, from tributum, that which is paid. In Judges the word records a compromise: Israel found the Canaanites profitable and left them in the land.
biblical_def: The law allowed it for cities far off: “if it make thee answer of peace, and open unto thee… all the people that is found therein shall be tributaries unto thee, and they shall serve thee” (Deu 20:11). Judges 1 records the tribes applying it where God had commanded otherwise. Zebulun “did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron… but the Canaanites dwelt among them, and became tributaries” (Jdg 1:30). Naphtali the same (Jdg 1:33). Of the Amorites, “the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed, so that they became tributaries” (Jdg 1:35). The chapter states the pattern outright: “when Israel was strong, that they put the Canaanites to tribute, and did not utterly drive them out” (Jdg 1:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tributary as paying tribute to another, either from dependence or for protection; subject; subordinate.
webster_full: TRIBUTARY, a. Paying tribute to another, either from dependence or for the purchase of peace, or for protection.
TRIBUTARY, n. One that pays tribute or a stated sum to a conquering power.
TRIBUTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another, in acknowledgment of subjection.
scriptures: And it shall be, if it make thee answer of peace, and open unto thee, then it shall be, that all the people that is found therein shall be tributaries unto thee, and they shall serve thee.
Jdg 1:28
And it came to pass, when Israel was strong, that they put the Canaanites to tribute, and did not utterly drive them out.
Jdg 1:30
Neither did Zebulun drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, nor the inhabitants of Nahalol; but the Canaanites dwelt among them, and became tributaries.
Jdg 1:35
But the Amorites would dwell in mount Heres in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim: yet the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed, so that they became tributaries.
corruption_summary: Judges 1 shows Israel taxing what God told them to remove, and the book's whole tragedy follows from the arrangement.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 1:28 is one of the saddest sentences in the Old Testament, and it turns on the word strong. When Israel was strong, they put the Canaanites to tribute and did not utterly drive them out. Strength was the opportunity for full obedience and became the occasion for a profitable compromise instead. The angel of the LORD delivers the verdict in the next chapter: ye have not obeyed my voice; wherefore I also said, I will not drive them out from before you; but they shall be as thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare unto you. Every cycle in the rest of the book grows out of that decision.

The corruption to name is the management of sin rather than the mortification of it. Israel did not adopt Canaanite religion at this stage; they simply found the Canaanites useful and arranged terms. Romans 8:13 gives the alternative in the strongest possible verb: if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. Mortify means kill. Sin kept under tribute pays for a while and then becomes a thorn and then a snare, exactly in the order Judges 2 predicts, and the man who has arranged terms with a besetting sin is usually strong at the moment he does it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mas (H4522), forced labour, tribute; yarash (H3423), to drive out, dispossess; moqesh (H4170), a snare.
roots_lines: Hebrew mas (H4522) — tribute, forced labour; Judges 1:28, 1:30, 1:35, Deuteronomy 20:11.
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to drive out, dispossess, inherit; Judges 1:28, Numbers 33:52.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, prevail; Judges 1:28, Joshua 1:6.
usage: “When Israel was strong… did not utterly drive them out” — the compromise named.
“The Canaanites dwelt among them, and became tributaries” — repeated tribe by tribe.
“All the people that is found therein shall be tributaries unto thee” — the law's allowance.

pos: n. (the back of a horse as a place of riding; in Scripture the posture of a royal messenger or an honoured man)
etymology: English horse + back. Riding is rare in the Old Testament narrative and always significant — the horse belongs to kings, messengers, and armies, not to ordinary travel.
biblical_def: A rider goes out to meet Jehu: “there went one on horseback to meet him, and said, Thus saith the king, Is it peace? And Jehu said, What hast thou to do with peace? turn thee behind me” (2Ki 9:18). Haman is compelled to lead his enemy in triumph: “Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city” (Est 6:11), and went home mourning with his head covered (Est 6:12). And the counter-decree rides out on the same animals: “sent letters by posts on horseback, and riders on mules, camels, and young dromedaries” (Est 8:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines horseback as the state of being on a horse; the posture of riding on a horse.
webster_full: HORSEBACK, n. The state of being on a horse; the posture of riding on a horse.
HORSEMAN, n. A rider on horseback; one who is skilled in riding.
POST, n. A messenger or a carrier of letters and papers; one that goes at stated times to convey the mail.
scriptures: So there went one on horseback to meet him, and said, Thus saith the king, Is it peace? And Jehu said, What hast thou to do with peace? turn thee behind me. And the watchman told, saying, The messenger came to them, but he cometh not again.
Est 6:11

Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.
Est 6:12
And Mordecai came again to the king's gate. But Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered.
Est 8:10
And he wrote in the king Ahasuerus' name, and sealed it with the king's ring, and sent letters by posts on horseback, and riders on mules, camels, and young dromedaries:
corruption_summary: Haman built a gallows for Mordecai and spent the morning leading Mordecai's horse, which is the book of Esther's method in one scene.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther 6 is the turning point and it is engineered entirely out of small things. The king cannot sleep; the book of records is read; the reader happens on the page where Mordecai exposed a plot and was never rewarded; Haman arrives early to ask for a hanging and is asked instead what should be done for the man the king delights to honour. He describes his own dream and is ordered to perform it on his enemy. The chapter contains no miracle and no mention of God, and it is impossible to read it as chance. Proverbs supplies the doctrine: the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's government is no less complete for being invisible. Esther is in the canon partly to teach believers to read their own lives, in which nothing parts and no fire falls. The sleepless night is the model: a small, unremarkable, entirely natural event standing at the hinge of a nation's survival. And the moral for the enemies of God's people is stated in the same chapter by Haman's own wife and wise men — thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him.

Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run, of a courier; Esther 8:10, 8:14.

usage: “Is it peace? And Jehu said, What hast thou to do with peace?”

“Sent letters by posts on horseback” — the counter-decree of Esther 8.

pos: n. pl. (instruments of scourging; the emblem of Rehoboam's policy toward his father's subjects)
etymology: Middle English whippe, of Germanic origin. Hebrew shot, a scourge. The word survives in Scripture almost entirely in one exchange, where it is set against scorpions — whips barbed or weighted to tear.
biblical_def: Rehoboam, following the young men, answers Israel's petition for relief with an escalation: “whereas my father did lade you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke: my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions” (1Ki 12:11), and he says it to their faces (1Ki 12:14; and 2Ch 10:14). The kingdom split within the hour: “What portion have we in David? neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: to your tents, O Israel” (1Ki 12:16). And the chronicle adds the deeper cause: “the king hearkened not unto the people; for the cause was from the LORD” (1Ki 12:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a whip as an instrument for driving horses or other beasts, or for correction, consisting of a lash tied to a handle.
webster_full: WHIP, n. An instrument for driving horses or other teams, or for correction, consisting of a lash tied to a handle, or of a handle and thong of leather.
SCOURGE, n. A whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord; an instrument of punishment or discipline.
SCORPION, n. In scripture, a scourge armed with points, so called from its severity.
scriptures: And now whereas my father did lade you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke: my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.

And spake to them after the counsel of the young men, saying, My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke: my father also chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.
Wherefore the king hearkened not unto the people; for the cause was from the LORD, that he might perform his saying, which the LORD spake by Ahijah the Shilonite unto Jeroboam the son of Nebat.

So when all Israel saw that the king hearkened not unto them, the people answered the king, saying, What portion have we in David? neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David. So Israel departed unto their tents.
corruption_summary: Rehoboam forsook the counsel of old men who had stood before his father and took the advice of men who had grown up with him, and lost ten tribes in a day.
corruption_paragraphs: First Kings 12 is a case study in counsel. The old men, who had stood before Solomon, told Rehoboam that if he would be a servant to this people and speak good words to them, they would be his servants for ever — a doctrine of authority the New Testament will restate in Mark 10 and 1 Peter 5. He forsook it for the counsel of the young men who had grown up with him, whose advice flattered his fear of appearing weak. The result was immediate and permanent. And verse 15 supplies the layer beneath: the cause was from the LORD, that He might perform the word spoken by Ahijah, so that a fool's decision executed a prophecy without excusing the fool.

The corruption to name is authority conceived as domination, which the New Testament forbids in the sharpest terms. The princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, said Christ, but it shall not be so among you. Peter tells elders to feed the flock, not as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples. Rehoboam's whips-and-scorpions speech is what leadership becomes when a man's chief concern is that he not be thought smaller than his predecessor. The old men were not offering him a technique for keeping power; they were describing what a king is for.
roots_summary: Hebrew shot (H7752), whip, scourge; aqrab (H6137), scorpion, a barbed scourge; ol (H5923), yoke.
roots_lines: Hebrew shot (H7752) — whip, scourge; 1 Kings 12:11, Proverbs 26:3, Nahum 3:2.
Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to chastise, discipline; 1 Kings 12:11, Proverbs 19:18.
usage: “My father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
“What portion have we in David?” — ten tribes gone within the hour.
“For the cause was from the LORD” — the folly executed a prophecy.

pos: adj. (without walls; of open villages, and of a Jerusalem so safe it needs none)
etymology: English un- + walled. In the ancient world an unwalled town was an undefended one; Scripture uses the condition both as vulnerability and, in prophecy, as the sign of a peace that needs no defences.
biblical_def: Moses distinguishes the two kinds of settlement: “All these cities were fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many” (Deu 3:5). Esther records that the Jews of the open country kept Purim a day earlier: “the Jews of the villages, that dwelt in the unwalled towns, made the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting” (Est 9:19). Ezekiel gives Gog's reasoning: “I will go up to the land of unwalled villages; I will go to them that are at rest, that dwell safely, all of them dwelling without walls, and having neither bars nor gates” (Eze 38:11). And Zechariah turns it into promise: “Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls for the multitude of men and cattle therein” (Zec 2:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unwalled as having no wall; not fortified or surrounded with a wall.
webster_full: UNWALLED, a. Having no wall; not surrounded or fortified with a wall.
WALL, n. A work or structure of stone, brick or other materials, raised to some height, and intended for a defense or security.
FENCED, a. Fortified; secured by a wall or other defense; as a fenced city.
scriptures: Deu 3:5
All these cities were fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many.
Est 9:19
Therefore the Jews of the villages, that dwelt in the unwalled towns, made the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting, and a good day, and of sending portions one to another.
And thou shalt say, I will go up to the land of unwalled villages; I will go to them that are at rest, that dwell safely, all of them dwelling without walls, and having neither bars nor gates,
Zec 2:4
And said unto him, Run, speak to this young man, saying, Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls for the multitude of men and cattle therein:
corruption_summary: Zechariah is told to stop the man measuring Jerusalem for walls, because the city's defence is to be the LORD Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Zechariah 2 is a vision about a surveyor. A young man goes out with a measuring line to take the breadth and length of Jerusalem, and an angel is sent running to stop him: Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls, for the multitude of men and cattle therein. Then the reason: For I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her. The city is to outgrow every wall a surveyor could plan, and it is to be defended by the presence of God rather than by masonry. This is the promise Ezekiel's Gog misreads as an opportunity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church's security has never been its defensibility. Gog's reasoning in Ezekiel 38 is perfectly sound on its own terms — unwalled villages, no bars, no gates, easy spoil — and it is why he is destroyed. The instinct to measure and wall is not wicked; Nehemiah built with a trowel and a sword, in his own hour and by God's command. But when God is the wall of fire, an added wall of stone is a smaller thing, and a people who trust the stone will find they have exchanged the glory in the midst for a perimeter.
roots_summary: Hebrew perazi (H6521), of open country, unwalled; chomah (H2346), wall; betach (H983), safely, securely.
roots_lines: Hebrew perazi (H6521) — belonging to an unwalled village; Deuteronomy 3:5, Esther 9:19, Ezekiel 38:11.
Hebrew perazah (H6519) — unwalled village, open country; Zechariah 2:4, Ezekiel 38:11.
Hebrew betach (H983) — safety, security, confidence; Ezekiel 38:11, Proverbs 1:33.
usage: “Beside unwalled towns a great many” — the open country of Bashan.
“I will go up to the land of unwalled villages” — Gog's reasoning.
“Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls” — and God the wall of fire.
